column4: There is a cognitive trap in changing our minds. If we don’t perceive a need to change our minds, then why would we ever open our eyes to look for change? Again, back to the poison analogy, if you cannot perceive that the poison is killing you, why would you stop consuming it?

column4: Some people believe that a person just must hit ‘rock-bottom’, then they will look at their lives and decide to change. Experience and psychology tell us we humans are more complex. There are many theories related to behavior change in the study of psychology, one highly regarded theory is the **Transtheoretical Model of Change** Developed in the late 1970s by James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente **\\[1\\].**
column5: Some people believe that as long as a person hits ‘rock bottom’, they will examine their life and decide to change. Experience and psychology tell us humans are more complex. There are many theories in psychological research on behavior change, and one of the most highly regarded is the **Transtheoretical Model of Change** (Transtheoretical Model of Change), proposed by James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente in the late 1970s**\\[1\\].**

column4: People may go through a cycle of six stages for change:
column5: People may cycle through six stages in the process of change:

column4: 1.  Precontemplation: There is no intention to change.
column5: 1.  Precontemplation stage: No intention to change.

column4: 2.  Contemplation: There is an intention to change in the near future.
column5: 2.  Contemplation stage: Intention to change in the near future.

column4: 3.  Preparation: Some steps have been taken to change.
column5: 3.  Preparation stage: Some steps toward change have already been taken.

column4: 4.  Action: The behavior has been changed for a short time.
column5: 4.  Action stage: Behavior has changed in the short term.

column4: 5.  Maintenance: The behavior has been changed and continues to be maintained.
column5: 5.  Maintenance stage: Behavior has changed and is being sustained.

column4: 6.  Termination: There is no desire to return to the previous behavior.
column5: 6.  Termination stage: No longer desires to return to previous behavior.

column4: There is no set length of time for how long any stage may take. Some people with respect to certain issues in their lives never meaningfully progress through the stages. In other instances, we can progress from stage 1 to 6 very expediently.
column5: There is no fixed length for how long each stage may last. For some issues in life, some people never meaningfully progress through these stages. In other cases, we can also move very quickly from stage 1 to stage 6.

column4: 1.  **Precontemplation**: He sees himself as a *firm* but *loving* parent. He believes raising his voice is necessary. He’s not considering changing. In fact, he might even justify it- “That’s how my dad raised me.”

column4: 2.  **Contemplation**: One day, after a long day at work, he snaps and yells at his young daughter harshly, louder and angrier than ever before. She flinches. Her lip trembles. She quietly walks away. In that moment… something **shifts**.

column5: ### Godly Sorrow and the Goodness of God

column4: While hitting rock-bottom is more a myth than a certain precondition to change, God can use sorrow to influence our minds.  God will use sorrow to bring us to repentance. He will convict us of our actions and the state of our lives and hearts to open our eyes to see our complete and total need of Him.
column5: Although the so-called hitting rock bottom is more of a myth than a necessary prerequisite for change, God can use sorrow to influence our minds. God uses sorrow to lead us to repentance. He will convict us of our actions and the state of our lives and hearts, opening our eyes to see our complete, absolute need for Him.

column4: Godly sorrow, or <u>the experience of sadness or distress that leads to a *metanoia*</u>, is not the same thing worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of sadness or distress, but the world offers no hope, only the relief and promise of death.
column5: Godly sorrow, or <u>the sorrow or painful experiences that lead to *metanoia*</u>, is not the same as worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is also the same sorrow or painful experiences, but the world offers no hope, only the promise of relief and of death.

column4: Sorrow is also different from suffering and grief.
column5: Sorrow is also different from suffering and grief.

column4: Suffering is the endurance of pain-physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual-especially when prolonged or intense.
column5: Suffering is the endurance of pain - physical, emotional, psychological, or spiritual - especially when it lasts a long time or is intense.

column4: Grief is a multifaceted emotional response to significant personal loss, especially relational or existential.
column5: Grief is the multifaceted emotional response to a significant personal loss, especially on a relational or existential level.

column4: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related ideas. In the human condition we will experience all three, we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring about death and destruction in our lives to teach us.
column5: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related concepts. As human beings we experience all three, and we can learn and grow through them, but God does not bring death and destruction into our lives in order to teach us.

column4: The scriptures say every good and perfect gift is from God above (James 1:17). He is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow will cause discomfort, but His discipline is just and loving. Just as a good father would not intentionally break his child’s arm to ‘teach him a lesson’, God will not inflict sickness or disease on His children to teach us.

Godly sorrow can be uncomfortable, but His discipline is just and loving. column4: ### Example of Worldly Sorrow vs Godly Sorrow
column5: ### Examples of worldly sorrow and godly sorrow

column4: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and he intentionally hit her, causing her to cry and leaving a red mark.
column5: A three-year-old boy and his two-year-old sister are playing in the yard. He is playing with a stick and deliberately hits her, making her cry and leaving a red mark.

column4: Their father hearing the commotion investigated and when he learned what his son did took the stick, broke it in half and tossed it away. He sent his son inside to think about what did and comforted his daughter.
column5: Their father hears the commotion and comes to check. After learning what his son has done, he takes the stick, breaks it in two, and throws it away. He sends his son inside to think about what he has done and comforts his daughter.

column4: The father coming inside to deal with his son found him crying. Asking him why he was crying his son said, “because you broke my stick”.
column5: The father comes inside to deal with his son and finds him crying. When asked why he is crying, the son says, "Because you broke my stick."

column4: The father’s reply was, “I’m sad that you are more concerned about your stick than you are about your sister who you hurt” and sent him back to his room for more reflection.
column5: The father replies, "What saddens me is that you care more about your stick than about the sister you hurt," and then sends him back to his room to continue reflecting.

column4: A few minutes later his son came back out and apologized. He said he was still sad because dad has broken his stick, and because he had hit his sister.
column5: A few minutes later, his son comes out again to apologize. He says he is still sad because Dad broke his stick, and also because he hit his sister.

column4: **Progress!**

column4: In this example the boy experienced both worldly sorrow, for his lost stick, and then eventually godly sorrow, for his hurt sister.

column4: Godly sorrow and God’s goodness are connected. God is a good father that will let us experience the consequences of our actions but will still stand beside us as we walk through those consequences.
column5: Godly sorrow is connected to God’s goodness. God is a good Father who will allow us to experience the consequences of our actions, but as we walk through those consequences, He still stands beside us.

column4: God's unrelenting goodness, to be willing to redeem us and restore us if we come to Him is a positive agent in our path of repentance. His goodness isn’t that we continue in sin, but that despite our sin He makes a way for us to be redeemed and experience His salvation.
column5: God’s relentless goodness—His willingness to redeem and restore us when we come to Him—is the positive driving force on our path of repentance. His goodness is not permission for us to continue sinning; rather, in spite of our sin, He makes a way for us to be redeemed and to experience His salvation.

column4: The Holy Spirit is the greatest agent for change mankind can engage with, and this is backed up by both the scriptures and by research. Research by “Lyons et al. column5: The Holy Spirit is the greatest agent of change with whom human beings can interact, a fact supported by both Scripture and research. Studies show, “Lyons et al. (2010) found that, in the course of substance abuse treatment and recovery, among subjects who experienced a spiritual awakening, the rate of complete abstinence at one-year follow-up was as high as 82%, whereas it was 55% among those who did not experience a spiritual awakening.” [2] Although people can initiate and bring about change, much more can be accomplished when we walk with the Spirit of God.

column4: ### David’s Example of Repentance
column5: ### David’s Example of Repentance

column4: Perhaps no account in the scriptures has a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin found in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to battle, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her, and they have an affair, resulting in Bathsheba's pregnancy.
column5: Perhaps no passage in Scripture presents a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin in 2 Samuel 11-12. The story begins with King David staying in Jerusalem instead of going out to battle, where he saw Bathsheba bathing. Although he knew she was the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David nevertheless had her brought to him and slept with her, resulting in Bathsheba becoming pregnant.

column4: To cover his actions, David recalls Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child's father. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go to his home with Bethsheba. David then arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front lines where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah's death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to cover up the pregnancy.
column5: To cover up his actions, David summoned Uriah back from the battlefield, hoping he would be with Bathsheba so it would appear that he was the child’s father. However, out of loyalty to his comrades, Uriah refused to go home to be with Bathsheba. So David arranged to have Uriah sent to the front lines, ultimately causing him to be killed in battle. After Uriah died, David quickly married Bathsheba to cover up the pregnancy.

column4: The Lord is displeased with David's actions and sends the prophet Nathan to confront him. When confronted by the prophet, David immediately admitted, "*I have sinned against the Lord*" (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly to God.
column5: The Lord was displeased with David’s actions and sent the prophet Nathan to confront him. When the prophet rebuked him, David immediately confessed, “*I have sinned against the Lord*” (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify his actions or make excuses. This confession was the first step in his repentance, directly acknowledging his transgression before God.

column4: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his complete ownership of his actions. He expresses grief not only for the sin itself but also for how it offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David displayed "*a broken and contrite heart,*" an essential part of true repentance (Psalms 51:17). This sorrow wasn’t superficial; he deeply grieved over the sin he committed and the hurt it caused. This depth of remorse was a sign that he wanted not only forgiveness but a changed heart.
column5: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me,*” show that he takes full responsibility for his actions. He grieves not only over the sin itself but over having offended God, saying: “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David exhibits a “*broken and contrite heart*,” which is an indispensable part of true repentance (Psalm 51:17). This sorrow is not superficial; he is deeply grieved over the sins he has committed and the harm they have caused. This depth of remorse shows that he longs not only for forgiveness but for a renewed heart.

column4: David asked God to “*Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me”* (Psalms 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would prevent him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than just apologizing, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow*” (Psalms 51:7). He recognized that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.
column5: David prays to God: “*Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me*” (Psalm 51:10). He seeks an inner change so that he will not repeat his mistakes. David does not merely apologize; he pleads for God to cleanse him, saying, “*Purge me, and I shall be whiter than snow*” (Psalm 51:7). He recognizes that only God can cleanse his heart and restore his joy.

column4: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways moving forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalms 51:12) demonstrates his hope to be aligned with God in every part of his life.
column5: David’s longing for spiritual renewal reflects his sincere commitment to walk in God’s ways going forward. He asks God for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalm 51:12), indicating his hope to be aligned with God in every aspect of life.

column4: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he was very sick. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).
column5: Although God forgave David’s sin, the Lord struck the child so that he became gravely ill. David fasted and prayed, pleading with God to spare the child’s life, but when the child died, David accepted the outcome (2 Samuel 12:15-23).

column4: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgressions. David’s decision to write down his plea for mercy, creating one of the Bible’s most enduring psalms, shows his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.
column5: In Psalm 51, we see both his personal prayer of confession and his public acknowledgment of his transgression. David’s decision to write down his plea for mercy resulted in one of the most enduring psalms in Scripture, showing his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm becomes a testimony to repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.

column4: David’s repentance journey was not simply about feeling sorry; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart transformation inscribed in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the Bible's most significant examples of genuine repentance.
column5: David’s journey of repentance was not merely feeling sorry; it was a profound change of heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart-change recorded in Psalm 51, David marked his sin as a lesson about God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the most important examples of genuine repentance in the Bible.
